text: On the morning of April 27th, 1986, Pripyat was one of the youngest cities in the Soviet Union.
say: On the morning of April twenty-seventh, nineteen eighty-six, Pripyat was one of the youngest cities in the Soviet Union.

text: The average resident was around 26 years old.
say: The average resident was around twenty-six years old.

v.label: average age of a Pripyat resident

text: The streets were full of strollers. The shops were better stocked than in most Soviet cities.
By that evening, almost fifty thousand people were gone.
They were told to pack for three days. None of them ever came back to live there.
Most videos will tell you Pripyat is a ghost town. But that's not really what it was.
Pripyat was a company town. Built for one employer. One purpose. One machine.

v.text:
One employer.
One purpose.
One machine.

text: And it wasn't the only one. The Soviet Union built a whole family of these cities. They were called atomgrads. Atom-cities.
say: And it wasn't the only one. The Soviet Union built a whole family of these cities. They were called atom grads. Atom cities.

text: This is the story of the most famous one, and the sisters it left behind.
In the late 1960s, the Soviet Union decided to build a nuclear power station in the marshy forests of northern Ukraine, near the old town of Chernobyl.
say: In the late nineteen sixties, the Soviet Union decided to build a nuclear power station in the marshy forests of northern Ukraine, near the old town of Chernobyl.

text: A power plant needs thousands of workers. And those workers need somewhere to live.
So, on February 4th, 1970, construction began on a brand-new town, about three kilometres from the plant site. It was named after the river that ran beside it. Pripyat.
say: So, on February fourth, nineteen seventy, construction began on a brand-new town, about three kilometres from the plant site. It was named after the river that ran beside it. Pripyat.

text: This is the key to understanding everything that came later. Pripyat didn't grow the way normal towns grow. No market square that slowly became a city over centuries.
It was designed on paper, all at once, around a single question. What does a nuclear plant need?
Engineers. Operators. Construction crews. And their families. So the city was built for them. And almost everyone there was, directly or indirectly, working for the plant.
In the West, we'd recognise the model. Hershey had chocolate. Pullman had railway cars. Pripyat had a reactor.
Pripyat wasn't a one-off. Across the Soviet Union, nearly every major nuclear plant came with its own satellite town.
Sosnovy Bor, for the Leningrad plant. Desnogorsk, for Smolensk. Kurchatov, for Kursk.
say: Sosnovy Bor, for the Leningrad plant. Desnogorsk, for Smolensk. Kurchatov, for Kursk.

text: Energodar, in southern Ukraine, built for what would become the largest nuclear plant in Europe. And Sniečkus, later renamed Visaginas, for the Ignalina plant in Lithuania.
say: Energodar, in southern Ukraine, built for what would become the largest nuclear plant in Europe. And Snieckus, later renamed Visaginas, for the Ignalina plant in Lithuania.

text: They followed a similar formula. A site close to the plant. Standardised prefab apartment blocks. A Palace of Culture for concerts and films. Sports complexes, swimming pools, cinemas.

v.title: The atomgrad formula
items: A site close to the plant

text: And a population that was young, educated, and relatively well paid.
Working in nuclear energy was prestigious. These towns were showcases. A little preview of the Soviet future.

v.tag: Sosnovy Bor, Russia — still a working atomgrad

text: For a young engineer in the 1970s, getting a flat in an atomgrad was a real step up.
say: For a young engineer in the nineteen seventies, getting a flat in an atom grad was a real step up.

text: Pripyat received official city status in 1979. By the mid-1980s, it had around forty-nine thousand residents.
say: Pripyat received official city status in nineteen seventy-nine. By the mid nineteen eighties, it had around forty-nine thousand residents.

text: It had schools and kindergartens. A hospital. A hotel.
A palace of culture. A stadium. An indoor swimming pool called Azure.
A river port. A large supermarket. And cafés along the water.
Because the residents were so young, the birth rate was very high. Some accounts describe roughly a thousand children being born there every year.
People who grew up there remember it fondly. The river beaches in summer. The forests. The feeling of living somewhere modern, and important.
The plant kept growing too. By 1983, four reactors were running, with two more under construction. Pripyat was planned to grow with them.
say: The plant kept growing too. By nineteen eighty-three, four reactors were running, with two more under construction. Pripyat was planned to grow with them.

text: But a company town has a weakness built into its foundation. When everything depends on one employer, everything is exposed to that employer.
In most company towns the danger is economic. The factory closes. The jobs disappear. The town slowly empties.
In Pripyat, the danger was physical. And it was three kilometres away.
At 1:23 in the morning, on April 26th, 1986, during a safety test, Reactor Number Four at the Chernobyl plant exploded.
say: At one twenty-three in the morning, on April twenty-sixth, nineteen eighty-six, during a safety test, Reactor Number Four at the Chernobyl plant exploded.

text: We won't go deep into the technical failure here. What matters for our story is what the city didn't know.

v.tag: Reactor No. 4 and its first shelter

text: April 26th was a Saturday. In Pripyat, life mostly carried on. Children went to school. People were outside. Some couples got married.
say: April twenty-sixth was a Saturday. In Pripyat, life mostly carried on. Children went to school. People were outside. Some couples got married.

text: The city's new amusement park, with its yellow Ferris wheel, was getting ready to open for the May Day holiday.

The workers at the plant knew something was badly wrong. And many people in Pripyat were those workers, and their families. But official information was minimal. And the decision to evacuate was delayed.
On the afternoon of April 27th, around thirty-six hours after the explosion, a radio announcement went out.
say: On the afternoon of April twenty-seventh, around thirty-six hours after the explosion, a radio announcement went out.

text: Residents were told they would be temporarily evacuated. Take documents. Essentials. Food for a few days.

v.text:
Documents.
Essentials.
Food for a few days.

text: More than a thousand buses arrived from Kyiv and the surrounding region. Within a few hours, a city of nearly fifty thousand people had been emptied.
Think about what that means for a company town.
In Pullman, or Fordlandia, decline took years. People had time to sell their homes, and say goodbye. In Pripyat, the employer that created the city ended it in a single afternoon.
Three days became forever. The flats, the toys, the photos, the furniture. All of it stayed exactly where it was.
Here's the part most people don't realise. When the residents left, the employer didn't.
The Chernobyl plant's other reactors went back into operation. The last one wasn't shut down until December 2000.
say: The Chernobyl plant's other reactors went back into operation. The last one wasn't shut down until December, two thousand.

v.sub: Chernobyl's last reactor is shut down

text: The plant still needed thousands of workers. But the workers no longer had a home.
For a while, the Azure pool stayed open for the clean-up workers, known as liquidators. But the city itself could never be lived in again.
So the Soviet Union did something remarkable. It built a new company town.
About fifty kilometres east, outside the most contaminated areas, construction began on a city called Slavutych.
And it was built in an unusual way. Different Soviet republics each designed and built their own district.
There's a Tallinn quarter. A Riga quarter. Vilnius. Baku. Yerevan. Tbilisi. Districts from Moscow, Leningrad, Belgorod, and Kyiv. Each with its own architectural style.
It was the last city the Soviet Union ever built. And in a way, it was Pripyat's second life. Many former residents and plant workers moved there.
And it faced the same old problem. One city. One employer. When the plant fully closed in 2000, Slavutych had to figure out what a company town does when the company is gone.
say: And it faced the same old problem. One city. One employer. When the plant fully closed in two thousand, Slavutych had to figure out what a company town does when the company is gone.

text: So what happened to the rest of the atom-city family?

text: Visaginas, in Lithuania, was built for the Ignalina plant. When Lithuania joined the European Union, it agreed to shut that plant down. The last reactor closed in 2009, and the town has been shrinking ever since. The classic company-town story. Slow, and economic.
say: Visaginas, in Lithuania, was built for the Ignalina plant. When Lithuania joined the European Union, it agreed to shut that plant down. The last reactor closed in two thousand nine, and the town has been shrinking ever since. The classic company town story. Slow, and economic.

text: Energodar, in southern Ukraine, is home to the Zaporizhzhia plant, the largest in Europe.
Since 2022, the town and its plant have been under Russian occupation. A reminder that an atom-city's fate is tied to its reactor, and to whoever controls that reactor.
say: Since twenty twenty-two, the town and its plant have been under Russian occupation. A reminder that an atom city's fate is tied to its reactor, and to whoever controls that reactor.

text: Others, like Sosnovy Bor and Desnogorsk in Russia, still function much as they were designed to. Towns that exist because a plant exists.
When we look at Pripyat today, we usually see a disaster. Radiation. Ruins. A frozen moment in 1986.
say: When we look at Pripyat today, we usually see a disaster. Radiation. Ruins. A frozen moment in nineteen eighty-six.

text: But look at it the way we look at every town on this channel. Pripyat was a promise. Come here, work for us, and we'll give you a modern life.
For about sixteen years, that promise was kept.
Every company town makes the same bargain. It gives you everything, but it depends on one thing. Most of the time, that dependence ends slowly. In Pripyat, it ended in one afternoon.
The Ferris wheel was supposed to turn for the first time on May Day. It's still waiting.
